What immediately comes to mind is that this would be entirely unconstitutional if as stated in the title. However, it doesn't appear to be exactly that.

  • First, its in the UK so I don't know whether it could be unconstitutional or not there.
  • Second, it appears to be applied to a limit set of circumstances "to recognise situations where women may have been unable to give consent". These appear to include "where someone is incapacitated through drink or drug", where “a suspect held a position of power over the potential victim - as a teacher, an employer, a doctor or a fellow gang member”, "where the complainant has mental health problems, learning difficulties or was asleep or unconscious at the time of the alleged attack", and "The new guidance also covers domestic violence situations and those where the complainant may be financially or otherwise dependent on their alleged rapist”,
  • Third, this doesn't appear to be a change in laws. That is, it doesn't change the situation at trial where you are presumed innocent until proven guilty. They still need to prove you guilty (I think). Rather, this appears to be a shift in the approach police take in questioning the accused. It's a set of guidelines for police forces.

I'm not suggesting this is necessarily a good thing or even necessary. The cases they describe this apply to are already illegal in most place (e.g., incapacitated or coercion from positions of power). The existence of consent has always been necessary. The problem of prosecuting rape is not one of consent, but one of "he said, she said". That is, her word that she didn't consent is insufficient to prosecute, as it should be. You can't convict criminals purely on the word of the accuser; there needs to be corroborating evidence. That's the source of the problem.

So changing the way police ask questions probably won't have any effect on convictions. The legal requirements of evidence haven't changed. It might have an effect on conviction rate if there have been cases with evidence available but the police didn't dig enough because of the way they asked questions. Perhaps it could lead to a few more convictions in that case simply by improving the police work, not by changing the laws. I'm skeptical it'll change much though.
